answer:
The first-line acute treatment for migraine recommended by the American Headache Society Consensus Statement, published in 2021 [American Headache Society, 2021], suggests that NSAIDs or triptans are generally effective. When these medications do not work, patients might consider combining a triptan with an NSAID, which is found to be more potent than either medication alone. For patients experiencing at least four migraines per month, preventive therapy should complement acute treatment [American Headache Society Consensus Statement, 2021]. Preventive treatments can help reduce the frequency and severity of migraine attacks over time.

Unfortunately, there seems to be no directly relevant clinical guidelines on treating acute low back pain available from these results. For that condition, the American College of Physicians recommends nonpharmacologic first-line treatment options, such as heat therapy or gentle exercise, in conjunction with NSAIDs if medication is necessary [American College of Physicians, 2017] — imagery should not be used without red-flag symptoms, such as trauma, weight loss for which there are no findings and neurologic deficits.

results.content: For acute migraine treatment, NSAIDs or triptans are first-line for most patients; combining a triptan with an NSAID is more effective than either alone. For patients with 4 or more migraine days per month, preventive therapy should be offered in addition to acute treatment.
results.citation: Acute Treatment of Migraine, American Headache Society, 2021

results.content: For acute low back pain, most patients improve regardless of treatment; first-line care is nonpharmacologic — heat, massage, or gentle activity — and NSAIDs if medication is needed. Imaging is not recommended without red-flag findings such as trauma, unexplained weight loss, or neurologic deficit.
results.citation: Noninvasive Treatments for Low Back Pain, American College of Physicians, 2017

metadata.title: Noninvasive Treatments for Low Back Pain
